title: Let the Dead Bury Their Own Dead
paragraphs:
Let the Dead Bury Their Own Dead
The Shocking Words of Jesus That Still Disturb Hearts Today
There are verses in Scripture that comfort us.
There are verses that heal us.
And then there are verses that stop us in our tracks and force us to wrestle with what we thought we knew about Jesus.
This is one of them.
A man approached Jesus with what seemed like a completely reasonable request.
A request most of us would have granted without hesitation.
A request that sounds honorable, loving, and deeply human.
Yet Jesus responded with words so startling that people have struggled with them for nearly two thousand years.
In Matthew 8:21-22 we read:
"Lord, first let me go and bury my father."
But Jesus said to him,
"Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead."
In the original Greek, Jesus says:

Ἀκολούθει μοι, καὶ ἄφες τοὺς νεκροὺς θάψαι τοὺς ἑαυτῶν νεκρούς
(Akolouthei moi, kai aphes tous nekrous thapsai tous heautōn nekrous)
Literally:
"Keep following Me, and allow the dead to bury their own dead."
At first glance it sounds harsh.
Almost insensitive.
How could the same Jesus who wept at Lazarus' tomb say something like this?
How could the Savior who honored parents appear to dismiss a son's responsibility to bury his father?
Many people read this passage through modern assumptions and miss what is happening.
The text never says the man's father had just died.
In first-century Jewish culture, "let me bury my father" was often an expression meaning:
"Let me stay with my family until my father dies someday, fulfill my obligations, receive my inheritance, settle my affairs, and then I will follow you."
In other words, the request was not necessarily about a funeral.
It was about postponement.
It was about delay.
It was about saying:
"Jesus, You can have my future... eventually."
The man wanted discipleship on his schedule.
Jesus demanded discipleship on God's schedule.
That changes everything.
Because suddenly this conversation is not about a funeral.
It is about priorities.
It is about divided hearts.
It is about the dangerous illusion that there will always be a better time to obey God.
How many of us have prayed versions of the same prayer?
"Lord, after I make more money."
"Lord, after I fix my life."
"Lord, after my children are older."
"Lord, after retirement."
"Lord, after I finish this season."
"Lord, after one more year."
Yet tomorrow keeps becoming next year.
And next year keeps becoming someday.
And someday becomes a lifetime.
Jesus knew something we often forget.
Delayed obedience is still disobedience.
The urgency of His call was not cruelty.
It was mercy.
Because He knew how easily human hearts become trapped by temporary things.
When Jesus said, "Let the dead bury their own dead," He used the word νεκρός (nekros) twice, but in two different senses.
The first "dead" refers to the spiritually dead.
Those not following Christ.
The second refers to the physically dead.
Jesus was saying:
"Let those who are spiritually dead handle matters of this dying world. You have been called into the Kingdom of God."
That interpretation aligns perfectly with the rest of Scripture.
Jesus was not condemning family responsibilities.
The Bible consistently commands believers to honor parents.
In fact, failing to care for family is condemned in Scripture (1 Timothy 5:8).
The issue was not family.
The issue was ultimate allegiance.
Jesus was revealing a truth many people still resist:
Nothing can take first place above Him.
Not possessions.
Not comfort.
Not reputation.
Not relationships.
Not inheritance.
Not tradition.
Not even the most understandable human excuses.
The call of Christ is absolute because Christ Himself is absolute.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Many people are not rejecting Jesus.
They are simply postponing Him.
They attend church occasionally.
They like inspirational Bible verses.
They appreciate Christian content.
They admire Jesus from a distance.
But there is always something standing between admiration and surrender.
A relationship.
A habit.
A career.
An addiction.
A fear.
An ambition.
A secret sin.
A future plan.
Something always whispers:
"Later."
But Jesus has always called people in the present tense.
Follow Me.
Not someday.
Not eventually.
Not after everything makes sense.
Follow Me now.
The tragedy is that many people spend years arranging life while neglecting eternity.
Building kingdoms that will not survive the grave.
Protecting reputations that will not matter before God's throne.
Chasing achievements that cannot save a soul.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly remind us how brief life truly is.
Psalm 90:12 says:

לִמְנוֹת יָמֵינוּ כֵּן הוֹדַע
(Limnot yameinu ken hoda)
"Teach us to number our days."
Not our years.
Not our decades.
Our days.
Because every day is a gift.
Every breath is borrowed.
Every heartbeat is grace.
And one day every excuse will expire.
The shocking thing about this story is not Jesus' response.
The shocking thing is that we see ourselves in the man.
We understand him because we are him.
We know what it feels like to delay surrender.
To negotiate with God.
To promise future obedience while protecting present comfort.
Yet Jesus still stands before every generation with the same invitation.
Not condemnation.
Not rejection.
Invitation.
Follow Me.
The Gospel is not a story about people cleaning themselves up before coming to God.
The Gospel is the story of God coming for people who cannot save themselves.
The Apostle Paul reminds us:
"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us." (Romans 5:8)
While we were still sinners.
Not after.
Not when we became worthy.
Not when we finally had everything together.
Jesus moved toward us first.
That is why our ministry theme matters so deeply:
Because the Bible is filled with scandal.
Moses the murderer.
Rahab the prostitute.
David the adulterer.
Peter the denier.
Paul the persecutor.
Broken people.
Failed people.
Messy people.
People whose stories should have ended in shame.
Yet Jesus rewrote every chapter.
Because grace is greater than scandal.
Redemption is greater than failure.
Mercy is greater than the worst thing you have ever done.
Perhaps that is why this passage unsettles us so much.
It forces a question none of us can escape:
What is currently delaying my complete surrender to Christ?
What am I asking Jesus to wait for?
What excuse have I protected for years?
And what if His call is still the same today?
Follow Me.
Right now.
Not because He wants to take life from you.
Because He wants to give you eternal life.
The greatest tragedy is not dying physically.
The greatest tragedy is being spiritually alive enough to hear His voice but continually refusing His invitation.
The good news is that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Still forgives.
Still restores.
Still redeems.
Still rewrites stories.
If this message challenged you, do not keep it to yourself.
What is one thing Jesus has been asking you to surrender?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is still telling Jesus, "Later."
And somewhere tonight, Jesus is still lovingly saying, "Follow Me."
The invitation has not changed. The only question is whether we will keep postponing the Author who is trying to rewrite our story.
